nameStory: Corn spurrey gets its name from its habit of growing as a pesky weed in corn fields and other grain crops. The word 'spurrey' comes from the Latin 'spergere,' meaning 'to scatter,' referring to how this plant spreads its tiny seeds far and wide across farmland.
description: Corn spurrey is a low-growing annual weed that forms sprawling mats or small cushions in disturbed soil. This European import rarely grows taller than 8-12 inches, with thin, needle-like leaves that radiate out from stem joints like tiny green fireworks. Its small white flowers are easy to miss, but the plant's distinctive whorled leaf arrangement and sprawling growth habit make it recognizable once you know what to look for.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, linear leaves arranged in whorls of 6-10 around each stem joint, feeling soft and slightly fleshy when you roll them between your fingers

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers with 5 petals, only about 1/8 inch across, clustered at stem tips and easy to overlook

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats with multiple branching stems that sprawl outward from a central point

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Slender, often sticky or slightly hairy stems that feel somewhat succulent when pinched

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Produces tiny black seeds in small capsules that split open when mature, scattering seeds widely

habitat: Look for corn spurrey in disturbed, sandy or gravelly soils, especially along roadsides, in agricultural fields, gardens, and waste areas. It thrives in poor, acidic soils where other plants struggle and is commonly found in coastal areas of New England where sandy conditions suit its preferences.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes with their characteristic whorled leaves becoming visible in disturbed soil.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and produce their tiny white flowers from June through August, often blooming continuously.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen and scatter while plants begin to turn brown and die back with the first frosts.
seasonality.winter: Plants are completely dead and gone, existing only as seeds waiting in the soil for next year's growing season.

funFact: Despite being considered a troublesome weed today, corn spurrey was actually cultivated as cattle fodder in parts of Europe for centuries because it's surprisingly nutritious and cattle love its taste!
confusionNotes: The whorled, needle-like leaves might remind you of small bedstraw plants, but corn spurrey's leaves are fleshier and the plant stays much lower to the ground. Unlike bedstraw, spurrey leaves feel soft and slightly succulent rather than rough or scratchy.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - corn spurrey isn't related to corn at all. The 'corn' in its name is an old European term for any grain crop, since this plant was commonly found growing as a weed among various cereal grains.
compareHints: Corn spurrey is the only member of its genus commonly found in New England, making it unique among the pink family for its distinctive whorled leaf arrangement. Most other pink family members in our region have opposite leaves in pairs, not the radiating whorls that make corn spurrey so distinctive.
